https://www.politico.eu/article/nigel-fa.text: LONDON — Over the past decade, Nigel Farage has ripped political conventions apart, dictated the debate on Brexit and immigration, and driven his party into contention to win the next general election. But now the hard-right Reform UK leader faces what may be the biggest challenge in a career suddenly engulfed by troubles. From a far more potent rival in new Prime Minister Andy Burnham to a resurgent Tory party, pressure over his finances, and a dubious gamble on a special election, Farage and his team are feeling the heat. And their poll ratings have started to slide. Advertisement Advertisement “Farage is facing something of a perfect storm,” said Tim Bale, professor of politics at Queen Mary University of London and an expert on the right in Britain. “But while he’s on the ropes he’s by no means on the floor, let alone out for the count.” Farage insists he won’t be “cowed” by what he describes as intimidation and says he is preparing for a general election as soon as this autumn, although Burnham has said he has no imminent plans to call one. It’s an open question whether the Burnham bounce in the polls and the dip in Farage’s fortunes mark a decisive shift in momentum in British politics or merely a blip. What is clear is that the challenges facing Reform are substantial, and growing. Farage’s side admits that Burnham has lifted the Labour government since he took office on July 20 and hurt Reform with a blizzard of policy pledges and energetic social media videos that have dominated media attention. Reform’s leader, meanwhile, has been beset by questions over whether he broke parliamentary rules by not declaring a £5 million donation. Last month he quit parliament to trigger a special election in his constituency of Clacton on the east coast of England, vowing to take on the establishment he says is trying to stitch him up over the furor. But with none of the mainstream parties willing to play ball, the contest has assumed an air of farce: Farage’s only well-known opponent is a candidate who goes by Count Binface, a serial joker who dresses up as a trash can. Advertisement Advertisement As if that weren’t damaging enough, the Conservative Party that Farage has spent much of his career tormenting is staging its own recovery in the polls, as leader Kemi Badenoch strengthens her position. Even the number of migrants arriving in small boats has fallen, robbing Reform of its signature attack line to use against the government. The result is a notable slide in the polls both for the party and for Farage himself. Polling pains According to POLITICO’s polling partners, London-based Public First, Farage’s net approval rating has dropped from -16 in early May to -21 at the end of July. Among people who voted Conservative in 2024 — a key target group for Reform — his rating has fallen by 15 points over the same period. “Reform has lost significant support among the people who historically voted Conservative since the local elections,” said Seb Wride, head of polling at Public First. “Rather than being able to get on the front foot during the early weeks of Burnham’s leadership, the Clacton by-election is making Reform seem less relevant, and Labour has been able to largely ignore them while defining what they stand for under new leadership.” In a slew of headline voting-intention polls in recent days, Burnham’s Labour has pulled level with Reform and in some cases taken the lead, ending 15 months of consistent national poll leads for Farage’s party. Andy Burnham walks near the White Cliffs of Dover in England during a visit to HM Coastguard Maritime Rescue Coordination Centre on Aug. 2, 2026. | Jack Taylor/ AFP via Getty Images “We have been here before. We have dealt with difficult moments before,” said Gawain Towler, a board member of Reform UK and the party’s former communications chief. The attacks on Farage over his financial arrangements are unfair, and come from questionable sources, he said, though they have caused damage even so. Advertisement Advertisement “There has been an impact and the Burnham bounce does also have an impact on the polls of course. The two things are happening together,” Towler said. “But what’s interesting is the impact these attacks are having on our supporters is very little because they expect the establishment to behave like this.” The great establishment stitch-up Public First’s analysis suggests there is truth to the idea that Farage’s core support has solidified as a result of his recent difficulties: During the same period that his overall approval rating has fallen nationally, from early May to the end of July, it has risen by 13 points among people who voted Reform at the last election in 2024. According to Towler, there is evidence that “the Establishment” is going after Reform with a series of underhanded leaks and attacks. That narrative — of a vengeful elite intent on punishing the people’s champion and the underdog — has proven powerful for populist leaders such as Farage, Donald Trump, Marine Le Pen in France and many others. Like Farage, however, Burnham is portraying himself as an outsider who is on the side of ordinary voters against the elite. The next election, whenever it comes, may be decided by which of these two can best embody the insurgent spirit. “Nigel Farage is the most scrutinized politician in British politics and he has been for quite a long time — because of what he represents,” Towler said. “He is the leader of a political party, one that threatens not just the political establishment but the establishment across the board.” Towler argued that the British establishment is trying to shake Reform’s confidence and soften it up for an election campaign, likening the assault to the prelude to the World War I Battle of Messines, with “heavy artillery for weeks and weeks, trying to break morale.” Advertisement Advertisement “If they manage to take Farage out, there’s a general election tomorrow. That’s what they’re trying to do,” he said. “They’re trying to break our morale as a party and I think you’ll find we have more morale, and we’re made of sterner stuff than they suppose.” Walking away Queen Mary’s Bale said that while Farage is in difficulty, his situation is “serious but not terminal — not yet anyway.” If polls worsen and the financial scandals deepen significantly, that could change, he said. “If he decides to throw in the towel — and given his record and his thin skin, nobody should rule out that possibility — Reform is in serious trouble.” Farage has history of walking away. He quit as leader of his previous party, the UK Independence Party, after losing his bid to win a parliamentary seat in 2015, only to be persuaded to return a few days later. He also stood down as Reform leader and announced he would be retiring from politics in 2021, but jumped back into campaigning when former PM Rishi Sunak called a general election in 2024. That comeback decision, according to Towler, was the moment Farage reconciled himself to the hard reality of challenging the political establishment to win power. “He knew it was going to be really hard. He knew that not just him, but a lot of other people around him — his friends, his long-term friends and allies and supporters — are also getting attacked,” Towler said. “And this will continue. We know it will continue. But we then say, hold on, this is our country. We can’t give up. How can we possibly give up?” Advertisement Advertisement

https://www.dw.com/en/bulgaria-fire-at-f.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5MVGA EMCO's owner has survived an assassination attempt and its factories and warehouses have been repeatedly targeted Image: Nikolay Doychinov/AFP Advertisement Bulgarian authorities are investigating a fire at a munitions storage facility operated by arms maker EMCO. Police say the blaze broke out Friday night and follows a similar incident at another EMCO site in August. EMCO's munitions are used in Ukraine and sabotage has not been ruled out, video images of the fire broadcast locally showed it illuminating the night sky near the village of Tsareva Livada. The full extent of the damage is not yet known but no casualties have been reported. "At present there is no danger to the population," said local police, adding that employees had been evacuated and the area cordoned off. EMCO has ruled out any possibility of human error in the incident. Bulgarian authorities investigating On Saturday, Bulgarian Interior Minister Ivan ​Demerdzhiev announced an investigation, saying, "We will review previous cases in which similar fires occurred in the warehouses of this company, as well as at other companies, in order ‌to look for a possible connection or a similar pattern." EMCO production facilities manager Slavcho Dimiev confirmed the fire as well, saying the site mainly ⁠stores ammunition, including a small quantity of medium-caliber rounds. Dimiev told reporters additional security measures should ⁠be considered to protect arms ​facilities. "If it is ultimately concluded that they [arms facilities] have been targeted," he said, "this is not an attack on a particular company alone; it is an attack on the national interest." Could VW's Osnabrück car plant pivot to arms production? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video EMCO fire latest of several attacks attributed to Russia NATO member-state Bulgaria has supported Kyiv's self-defense efforts since Russian forces invaded Ukraine on February 24, 2022. And EMCO, like other European arms manufacturers, has been the target of repeated sabotage . The company is run by Bulgarian arms dealer Emilian Gebrev, the survivor of an assassination attempt that authorities there say was carried out by Russian operatives. Three Russian nationals were charged over the incident. In 2024, ​Bulgaria also issued arrest warrants for six Russian nationals that prosecutors say were involved in the destruction of EMCO arms depots storing munitions set for export to Ukraine ⁠and Georgia ​between 2011 and 2020. At the time, prosecutors argued that they had uncovered links between the attempt on Gebrev, sabotage at Bulgarian arms depots and explosions at a munitions depot in the Czech Republic in 2014. Arms manufacturers previously targeted Friday's fire at EMCO echoes a number of recent attacks targeting European arms makers supplying Ukraine. On August 13, the KNDS Ammo Italy arms manufacturing facility outside Rome was rocked by an explosion. Although the Italian government said it had no reason to believe that Russia was behind the attack, the Franco-German defense company said the incident was under investigation. On September 3, incendiary devices were thrown near the Munich headquarters of defense technology company Rohde & Schwarz. EMCO's Gebrev is not alone in being targeted either. In 2024, US and German intelligence uncovered a Russian plot to assassinate Armin Papperger , the CEO of Germany's largest arms manufacturer, Rheinmetall . In all instances, Russia has denied involvement, calling accusations, European war mongering. https://www.euronews.com/2026/09/24/russ.text: According to a report by the UN Security Council's Multilateral Sanctions Monitoring Team (MSMT), between 15,000 and 30,000 North Korean workers were present in Russia at the end of 2025.Up to 1,000 of them were employed at strategically important facilities, including defence plants, steelworks and shipbuilding capacities.The Ukrainian outlet "Ukrainska Pravda" also confirmed that up to 25,000 North Korean citizens are working on drone production in the Alabuga special economic zone in Tatarstan, where Russian versions of Iran's Shahed drone are assembled.Radio Liberty cites similar data, noting that North Koreans are registered as "students" in order to bypass UN sanctions that prohibit the use of DPRK labour abroad.In 2025 Russia issued more than 36,400 visas to North Korean citizens, of which 35,800 were student visas.Where North Koreans workWorkers from North Korea are now reportedly spread across Russia, from traditional employment regions in the Far East (Vladivostok, Khabarovsk and Sakhalin) to newer destinations such as Moscow, Saint Petersburg and Irkutsk.Tatarstan has become the main centre of their employment, in particular the Alabuga special economic zone, which features in most investigations as a key hub for assembling strike drones.It is here, according to Current Time and Radio Liberty, that North Korean workers staff assembly lines producing drones used by Russia to attack Ukrainian cities and infrastructure.Sanctions evasion schemeAlthough UN Security Council sanctions have banned the export of North Korean labour since 2017, Moscow and Pyongyang have built an entire ecosystem for circumventing these restrictions, the MSMT report notes.North Koreans are being registered en masse on student and tourist visas, which allows their real status to be concealed and their work at Russian companies to be legalised.According to reports, Russian legislation was amended to create legal loopholes that enabled "students" to receive income officially.The report also describes cases in which Russian universities were bribed to arrange fictitious study programmes, as well as the role of intermediaries from third countries, including Belarus, which help organise entry and distribute the workforce.This points to a systemic scheme that allows Pyongyang to earn millions of dollars and enables Russia to plug labour shortages in strategic industries.Control and confiscated wagesAccording to MSMT, the working conditions of North Korean labourers in Russia remain extremely harsh and are fully controlled by the Pyongyang authorities.The average annual income of such workers is around $7,500 (€6,593), but almost all of this is seized by Pyongyang.The report notes that in 2025 alone North Korea received up to 800 million dollars from the labour of its citizens abroad. These funds, the report stresses, are channelled into financing the country's nuclear and missile programme.The workers in effect live under constant surveillance by DPRK security services: their movements are strictly restricted, contact with Russian citizens is forbidden, and they are housed in closed dormitories to which outsiders have no access.Human-rights activists describe these conditions as "slavery", citing the absence of freedom, isolation and the people's complete dependence on the regime. These findings are reported (source in Russian) by "Radio Liberty" (RFE/RL) and "Current Time", which underline the systematic exploitation of North Korean citizens at Russian enterprises.Juche ideology at the service of Moscow's imperial ambitionsIn October 2024, intelligence services in South Korea, the United States and Ukraine began reporting that thousands of Pyongyang's soldiers were being sent to Russia.At the BRICS summit that same month, Russian President Vladimir Putin acknowledged the presence of North Koreans, but did not specify the purpose of their deployment.Russian military officials later confirmed that North Koreans were being used to help counter Ukraine's successful incursion into the Kursk region, which began in August 2024.Kim's regime subsequently established large-scale deliveries of arms and ammunition to Russia: artillery shells, ballistic missiles, small arms and artillery systems, and also sent military instructors.The money Pyongyang receives is spent on purchasing more powerful weapons, a massive housing and industrial construction programme and, experts believe, on developing its nuclear programme, where Moscow may also be providing expert advice.Why is Russia using North Korean labour?Russia is facing an acute labour shortage because of its war against Ukraine and mobilisation.North Koreans have become one means of filling staff gaps at defence-industry plants, especially in the drone sector, which requires large numbers of low-paid workers.German international broadcaster Deutsche Welle notes that cooperation between Moscow and Pyongyang intensified after Kim Jong Un's visit to Russia and agreements to expand military and industrial cooperation.But the use of North Korean labour at Russian defence plants has sparked concern:The United States, South Korea and Japan see this as a violation of UN sanctions;human-rights organisations highlight the exploitation of people and the funding of North Korea's nuclear programmes;experts warn that the cooperation boosts the military potential of both countries.What this means for the war in UkraineRussia launches hundreds of drones against Ukrainian territory every day. Moscow is now banking on mass production of cheap UAVs that can operate in swarms and overwhelm Ukrainian air defences.The use of more powerful, faster jet-powered drones is also expanding, and countering them is particularly challenging.The large-scale production of drones, in which North Korean workers are involved, directly increases the intensity of these attacks.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text: A drone view shows the mangled remains of the ancient cottonwood tree where activists staged a tree-sit to protest the construction of the US-Mexico border fence, in Lochiel, Arizona. Photograph: Rebecca Noble/Reuters View image in fullscreen A drone view shows the mangled remains of the ancient cottonwood tree where activists staged a tree-sit to protest the construction of the US-Mexico border fence, in Lochiel, Arizona. Photograph: Rebecca Noble/Reuters US immigration Despair after 200-year-old ‘grandmother’ tree toppled for Trump’s border wall: ‘It crushes your heart’ Protesters spent months occupying an ancient cottonwood. Then a tense standoff with US border patrol came to a head Douglas Main Sat 10 Oct 2026 16.57 EDT Last modified on Sat 10 Oct 2026 16.58 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A 200-year-old cottonwood tree near the US-Mexico border , known as the “grandmother”, has been destroyed to make way for the construction of Donald Trump ’s border wall, despite a months-long effort by protesters trying to save it. In late July, land defenders began a tree-sit in the ghost town of Lochiel, Arizona , taking turns occupying a platform high in the tree’s canopy. The group remained there for more than 70 days. Protesters occupy 200-year-old tree at US-Mexico border to stop its destruction: ‘She’s our Statue of Liberty’ Read more Then, on Monday at dawn, more than 80 federal agents swarmed the protesters’ camp, which is located on private land, making arrests and preventing people from reaching the cottonwood. Some agents in a steel basket on an extendable crane lift forcibly removed the person in the tree platform, according to videos and photos shared on social media and descriptions of people there at the time. Others were shoved and tackled as they tried to rush toward the tree to prevent its destruction, according to witnesses. Contractors with Fisher Sand & Gravel, a company building this section of wall, then used an excavator to push over the tree , which cracked and crashed to the earth. Land defenders shrieked, cried and yelled at the federal agents. “Seeing that – it crushes your heart,” said Erick Meza, the Sierra Club’s Borderlands coordinator who has been working to save the trees for months, beginning with a series of letters to US Customs and Border Protection (CBP). “That tree brought a lot of people together,” he said. Now, he added, “there’s a community response of outrage. People are pissed off.” The cottonwood’s toppling was filmed by a team from Turning Point USA , the far-right political group, who appeared to be embedded with border patrol and allowed free access to roam throughout the closed off public road. View image in fullscreen A tree-sitter on 29 July 2026 in the ancient cottonwood tree at the US-Mexico border in Lochiel, Arizona. Photograph: Rebecca Noble/Reuters One of the land defenders had scaled another ancient cottonwood tree situated right on the border with Mexico. On Thursday, CBP and Mexican police, who have been present for several days and visibly working with American authorities, removed the tree-sitter’s platform, food and water supplies, according to Alex Chabbott, a land defender who has been present at the camp on and off for over a month. Late on Friday, the tree-sitter came down on their own volition after not being resupplied for several days. We’re not going anywhere. We are rooted, like the grandmothers The agents involved include border patrol officers, part of CBP, and a special forces tactical unit called Bortac , whose self-described purpose is to “respond to terrorist threats”. The tree-sit began shortly after contractors knocked over and killed three other ancient cottonwood trees nearby on 27 July. Two 30ft-tall walls are being built throughout this area, known as the San Rafael valley, a remote and once idyllic high elevation prairie where the movie Oklahoma was filmed. The valley, and the Patagonia and Huachuca mountains on either side of it, form one of the most important regional wildlife corridors between the US and Mexico, providing passage to animals including jaguars , ocelots, bears and even beavers and porcupines in recent years. Already, government contractors have finished 88 miles (140km) of secondary wall, which is a second 30ft fence set at some distance from a primary wall of the same height. Another 444 miles of secondary wall are under construction, according to DHS , much of that in Arizona, using billions of dollars allocated by Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act. View image in fullscreen Members of the Nogales fire department use a cherrypicker to remove a platform from another tree on the border with Mexico, leaving a protester stranded. Photograph: Rebecca Noble/Reuters Protesters say that construction in the area is progressing rapidly, 24 hours a day. In recent days, Fisher Sand & Gravel has completed the secondary wall, which includes placing 30ft steel panels within a trench filled with rebar and cement, along a part of the private property where the camp is located, including up to the point where the tree stood. These trees, which depend on a regular supply of water underground, are a hallmark of riparian forests, an endangered ecotype throughout Arizona and the south-west, said Russ McSpadden, an advocate with the Center for Biological Diversity. The ecological importance of these trees is one of the animating factors behind the land defenders. Water use for wall construction has depleted wells throughout the south-west, threatening natural features such as Quitobaquito Springs . CBP does not say how much current construction uses, but in 2008 it estimated a smaller wall nearby could use up to 710,00 gallons per mile for construction; the current project likely uses more, as it is larger. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every day Sign up to Headlines US Get the most important US headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morning after newsletter promotion ‘We are starting a movement’ Since Monday, dozens of land defenders have been arrested , many for entering the road between the private property and the border, which was ordered closed by federal authorities in late September due to wall construction. Protesters have been doing prayers in the road near the tree every morning. Some of those arrested were physically hit and came back with bruises and black eyes, Chabbott claimed. Several more people attempted to use nonviolent tactics to halt or delay construction, including one woman who locked herself to a cement truck on 7 August, according to videos shared on social media. View image in fullscreen Protesters face off with US border patrol as Fisher Sand & Gravel construction crews work on 8 October 2026. Photograph: Rebecca Noble/Reuters The protester was sprayed in the face with mace and wrestled by several agents, and her limbs forced into painful positions, according to witnesses and social media videos. The truck was later driven away while the land defender was still attached, and cut from the vehicle later that evening, according to witnesses. She is now in custody, according to what authorities have told the land defenders’ lawyers. That tree brought a lot of people together. People are pissed off Julia Butterfly Hill, who spent two years living in a redwood in California’s Humboldt county in the late 1990s, said she was horrified to see how roughly border patrol treated this woman on a livestreamed video, she said. This land defender’s courage and commitment to nonviolent resistance in the face of brutality “brought tears to my eyes”, Butterfly Hill said. “She’s a hero of the highest order.” CBP did not respond to a request for comment about this and other clashes, but has previously said that walls in areas like this will help combat unauthorized immigration. The sheriff of Santa Cruz county, David Hathaway, who did not respond to a request for comment for this story, has previously said a wall in this area is senseless since this remote valley has no history of significant illegal activity. Fisher Sand & Gravel did not respond to a request for comment. View image in fullscreen A drone view shows the remains of two other ancient cottonwood trees in Lochiel, Arizona, on 27 July. Photograph: Rebecca Noble/Reuters In a press conference on 8 October, Adelita Grijalva, a congresswoman who represents the area, said she was “heartbroken” about the loss of the “grandmother” trees, and said she plans to try to introduce a bill that will revoke the DHS’s ability to waive any and all laws in building border infrastructure. The tree-sit began shortly after contractors knocked over and killed two other ancient cottonwood trees nearby on 27 July. In felling the tree, the contractors and federal agents “try to break us, but we are not broken”, said Kate Scott, one of the leaders of the tree-sit. “We are starting a movement, and we’re not going anywhere. We are rooted, like the grandmothers.” Explore more on these topics US immigration Arizona US-Mexico border Trump administration Donald Trump US politics Trees and forests news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed US news US politics Midterms 2026 World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cvde.text: Image source, Reuters Image caption, Large demonstrations descended into disorder in Paris and across France on Saturday By Jamie Whitehead Â and Â Gabriela Pomeroy Published 22 October 2026, 14:02 BST Updated 1 hour ago Paris is extending a partial curfew restricting movement in parts of the city until Monday, as Marseille and Lyon impose a total ban on protests this weekend. The Louvre, Orsay and Picasso museums in the French capital will also be closed on Saturday as more demonstrations are expected. France is still reeling from major disorder at the weekend, when large protests against the high cost of living and school conditions were overshadowed by riots and looting that saw business and historic buildings destroyed. In other parts of the country where protests have not been banned completely, only authorised union demonstrations will be allowed on Saturday, President Emmanuel Macron said. Interior Minister Jean-Didier Berger said police deployments would be increased by 20% compared to last weekend, after the government was accused of being blindsided by the scale of the unrest. France's justice minister said on Thursday that 217 people had been jailed over last weekend's disorder after being convicted in fast-track trials, with that number expected to rise. GÃ©rald Darmanin said 2,700 people had been arrested across France and more than 1,000 have appeared in court. Half of those detained had no prior criminal record, he said, according to Le Figaro newspaper. Police in Paris said its curfew in Place de la RÃ©publique, where protesters gathered last weekend, and the Les Halles shopping area will be extended until Monday. Movement will be prohibited in both areas from 23:00 local time (21:00 GMT) until 06:00 the following morning, the prefecture for the capital city said, adding that it had been ordered by Interior Minister Laurent NuÃ±ez and Prime Minister SÃ©bastien Lecornu. Public transport Marseille will be suspended on Saturday to try to prevent a repeat of the riots in the city. The city saw some of the worst violence last weekend and damage to more than 500 businesses. The prefecture for the RhÃ´ne region - which covers Marseille - said a curfew for minors would be extended to the entire population overnight on Saturday 24 October, from 23:00 until 05:00 (21:00 - 03:00 GMT). Similar announcements have been made in Nice in the south, Toulon on the south coast, the centre of Rouen in the north-west, and Grenoble in the east. Macron met intelligence services and ministers on Thursday, to prepare for the next national day of protests on Saturday. "The general recommendation is that there should be no demonstrations. Those who want to continue to demonstrate, when they are trade union organisations, will have alternative routes proposed by the prefects," the French president announced. "When they're not union organisations, wherever possible, they'll be banned." He attacked what he called "political and even seditious acts organised by far-left groups that aim to bring down the Republic". Curfews were imposed in several cities in the aftermath of the weekend rioting, and Macron said the government wanted a return to calm. The gilets jaunes (yellow-vest) movement was behind many of last weekend's protests and Paris authorities have said several of their proposed marches have been banned. Partial curfews variously restricting the movement of young people and gatherings have been in place this week in cities including Marseille, Bordeaux, Nice and Lyon in the south as well as Lille and other towns in the north. Prime Minister SÃ©bastien Lecornu promised a "massive" deployment of police officers this week to deal with any unrest this weekend, but some officers have told French media they are not trained to deal with large crowds. Image source, Reuters Image caption, Unrest spread across several French cities last weekend, including the capital Paris Around 550,000 people took part in demonstrations on 17 October to protest rising fuel prices and the cost of living, which have escalated after weeks of student protests . Marches were largely peaceful and took place in several major French cities, including Paris, backed by unions, gilets jaunes and student groups. But they were marred by scenes of violence, looting and destruction. Lyon's tourism office was set on fire by demonstrators during last weekend's protests. In the city of Limoges, the clock tower and parts of the roof of the ornate city hall were engulfed in flames before collapsing on Saturday. A second suspect aged 66 was arrested on Thursday, after a man in his 30s was detained on suspicion of the attempted murder of police officers who were in the city hall when the fire started. The iconic Place de la RÃ©publique was vandalised in the capital, Paris, when groups of rioters took over parts of the city, wreaking havoc. The unrest has come as Macron enters the final months of his presidency, with elections scheduled for 18 April and 1 May next year.
